4104.heavy: Not framed as weight. Three classes of 'syllabifier' (p.84, 86-87): 'full vowel' = any vowel other than ə ə̣ (a ạ i ị u ụ); 'weak vowel' = ə ə̣, and 'weak syllabifiers' also include the second consonant of a root- or suffix-final cluster (t in ʔawt, x in -ilx) and lexical suffixes/clitics of shape C or CC (-c 'mouth', -k 'back', -qs 'nose', _ƛƛ 'and then'); 'strong syllabifiers' = a closed set of suffixes (-ʔúl 'real, par excellence', -sút reflexive, -uƛ̓ 'step-relative', -uƛ̓ 'always') that attract the stress regardless of the rules. Full vowels before ʔ act as weak 'as a rule' (p.86). Weak syllabifiers are counted but cannot receive shifted stress.
4104.dflt: Words with weak vowels only: 'the stress falls, as a rule, on the first vowel' (p.85 sec. 2.2: tə̣́q-ən 'to touch', ǧə́l-ǧəl 'strong', sə́k-mən 'whip'); when such a root is followed by a suffix with a full vowel the base is the (first) full vowel of the suffix (qə̣l-ƛkán 'I am bad', p.86). With no strong suffix the base is the lexically stressed full vowel of the root.
4104.prule: Lexical: one stress per word (word plus enclitics); its underlying position is phonemic, contrastive in root minimal pairs (mạ́qaʔ 'snow' vs. mạqáʔ 'poison onion', ƛ̓ámin 'fur' vs. ƛ̓amín 'axe'), and the 'counting base' for every derived form is the lexically stressed full vowel of the root (usually but not always its first full vowel, cf. qan̓ím) or, when present, the last of a closed set of 'strong' suffixes that always attract stress.
4104.srule: van Eijk 1981 writes one stress per word ('In polysyllabic Lillooet words one syllable is stressed', p.84) and does not mention secondary stress (pp.84-90 read). Later work on the same data and new recordings: secondary stress, unmarked in van Eijk's transcriptions because predictable, falls on the pre-tonic counting-base vowels, i.e. the heads of the trochaic feet parsed left-to-right from the root's stressed vowel up to the primary (ʔùxʷalmíxʷ-kan 'I am an Indian', cùƛ-un̓-tùmuƛ-káƛ̓ap 'you folks pointed at us'); confirmed acoustically (small F0/duration difference from primary); post-tonic or final secondary stress not reported.

4106.dq: Stress (§2.7.) is not contrastive and has a rather minor role in the articulation of words, while intonation patterns (§2.8.) are far more important [p. 37] ... primary stress is assigned to the penultimate syllable of polysyllabic lexical stems and falls on the single syllable of monosyllabic stems. When lexical items contain more than one stem, stress is assigned separately to each stem. [p. 96]
4106.dloc: §2.7 'Stress' pp. 96-99 (§2.7.1 nouns pp. 97-98, §2.7.2 verbs pp. 98-99 incl. footnote 16 and reduplication/imperative examples (2.109)-(2.110) p. 99); chapter-2 overview remark p. 37; negation-particle remark p. 424; §2.8 Intonation begins p. 99.
4106.prule: Stress is non-contrastive and assigned inside the lexical stem, not counted from the edge of the phonological word: primary stress on the penultimate syllable of a polysyllabic lexical stem (sole syllable of a monosyllabic stem); the fossilised common-noun prefix n(V)- is counted as part of the noun stem, so nouns come out word-penultimate ([ˈni.jo], [ni.ˈte.rix]); in verbs the obligatory subject/mood prefix is disregarded and stress falls on the first syllable of the verb stem ([imˈвulem] 3σ penult, [nitiβˈlem] 3σ final, [isˈɣam] 2σ final); reduplicated stems are stressed on the first syllable of the stem ([nit.ˈmal.ma.lu] 4σ antepenult); each stem of a compound carries its own stress ([ne.ˈɣel.ˈβas]). Word-level position therefore follows morphological structure (stem edge; prefix class), not syllable count.
4106.srule: No secondary stress described for single-stem words (§2.7 gives one primary stress per stem; auditory analysis). More than one stress per word only through morphology: each stem of a compound is stressed ('these compound nouns are stressed twice': [ˈniliβ-ˈmaβus], [ne.ˈɣel.ˈβas]) and imperatives are stressed on both the subject/mood prefix and the stem-initial syllable ([ˈkam.ˈtuɸ] 'go away!'); the post-verbal negator si carries a stress weaker than the verb's (p. 424).

4107.dq: Word stress is typically indicated by a contrast in greater force (compared to unstressed syllables), by higher pitch, and by minute lengthening of the vowel. [p.52] ... Where a grammatical phrase contains more than one stress group [§6.3], phrase stress occurs on the final stressed syllable of the phrase. [p.53]
4107.dloc: p.52 sec.5.2-5.2.1 and p.58 sec.5.3.2, both read (pp.71, 77); p.53 sec.5.2.2 and p.54 sec.5.2.3 and p.80 sec.5.8 read in the scan extract (pp.72-73, 99); dialect-scope sentence p.40 sec.4.5 with fn.12. Image-only scan
4107.prule: Penultimate syllable of the lexical root/stem, quantity-insensitive. Every vowel is a syllable nucleus (VV sequences are two syllables; stress on the first, p.51), and the author explicitly rejects a moraic/vowel-length analysis as uneconomical (p.52). Prefixes and the consonantal enclitics -k -t -n -h -l do not move stress; the syllabic plural enclitic -ro and paragogic -e are extrametrical; the syllabic suffix -i shifts stress to the new penult (hefa-i-k, p.54). Stress never falls on the final syllable of the root (p.58).
4107.srule: None inside the word: one stress per stress group (root penult); pre-penultimate syllables, proclitics and cliticised roots are unstressed, and strings of cliticised roots show only two levels, stressed vs unstressed (Grimes 1991 pp.53-54, 89). 'Secondary stress' arises only in the vocative calling pattern: enclitic -é takes the main stress and length and the root's penult keeps secondary stress, e.g. ama-n-é 'father!' (p.80 sec.5.8.2).

4108.sec_rule: When primary stress is displaced from the penult by morphology (verbs with unstressable L-suffixes or -wa; host + enclitic copula; plural imperative + L-suffix), the vowel of the open penultimate syllable of the word (or host+copula unit) is lengthened; Molin analyses this compensatory prominence of the canonically stress-bearing penult as secondary stress ('Rule 2'), e.g. húllū-lan [ˈhulluːlan] 'they gave us', gúrgā=le [ˈgurgaːle]. Realised as duration; one such prominence per word, to the right of the primary; absent in words with regular penultimate stress; may fail when a pretonic long ā is retained (Rule 3).
4108.sec_quote: if stress cannot be penultimate, the vowel in the penultimate syllable is lengthened as long as that syllable is open. This is apparently a synchronic mechanism of lending the penultimate (i.e. canonically stress-bearing) syllable prominence to compensate for its lack of stress. This type of prominence can be considered secondary stress.

Billington's stress survey (pp. 73-74) covers Nilotic in general: Tucker & Bryan 1966 make 'passing mention of stress occurring on verb stems', and explicit no-contrastive-stress statements exist for Turkana (Heine 1980: 44) and for Otuho (Coates 1985: 102), Lokoya's closest relative (64.5 % lexical similarity per Vossen), but no such statement exists for Lokoya itself. The open Rosetta excerpts of Vossen's phonology notes for Bari, Karimojong and Teso/Turkana contain no occurrence of 'stress', 'accent' or 'Betonung' (a full-text search this stage) and follow a Consonants/Vowels/Tone scheme, so the unopened Lokoya notes at pp. 189-193 most likely have the same shape; unverified.

4113.heavy: As stated: 'a low or mid to high vowel sequence' (ai, au, ei, ou; rising diphthong) is 'always' stressed on its first vowel, so it forms one stress-bearing unit; the base rule is 'measure-penultimate stress (Schütz 1976)', a measure/mora count under which Lau raíca is penultimate. Long vowels are never stated to attract stress in these communalects: the only length-stress statements are the transcription convention (sec. 1.2, diss. p. 4: underlying long vowels surface long 'except when preceding an unstressed vowel') and the phonotactic constraint 'disallowing a long vowel before an unstressed syllable', 'common to all Fijian languages' (sec. 4.5.1, diss. pp. 154, 156), neither of which is a stress-placement rule. The CVV coding therefore rests on the diphthong clause alone.
4113.prule: Stress on the penultimate unit of the word ('the penultimate stress rule'), which Geraghty identifies with Schütz's (1976) 'general principle of measure-penultimate stress', a measure/mora (vowel) count; in every communalect sampled except Lau, a low-or-mid + high vowel sequence (ai, au, ei, ou) is 'always' stressed on its first vowel (ráica 'see it', ráuta 'enough'), so a rising diphthong behaves as one heavy unit carrying the stress on its first mora rather than being counted vowel by vowel (Lau raíca).

4114.dq: Camuno phonological words contain one primary stress. All monosyllabic content words are stressed as in (59). (p. 56) [...] Evidence for the phonological word comes from three different sound patterns: stress, height harmony, and final obstruent devoicing. As already discussed, each content word has one primary stress which typically falls on the final syllable, but may also occur on the penult o…
4114.dloc: Cresci 2014 §3.3 'Camuno stress patterns', p. 56; §3.5 'The phonological word in Camuno', p. 63; §3.6 'The metrical foot in Camuno', p. 64.
4114.heavy: Explicitly not weight-sensitive (p. 59): 'kun.tin.tí „sop‟ and for.men.tú „maize‟ have stress on final vowels, though the penult and antepenult are closed/heavy syllables. In cases where exceptional stress is involved, there is no sign of weight sensitivity either, e.g. kalýz n „soot‟, with exceptional penultimate stress and a heavy final syllable.'
4114.prule: Right-edge rule conditioned on the final segment, quantity-insensitive: one primary stress per phonological word. Stress falls on the final syllable when the word ends in a consonant or in a vowel other than /ɔ/ (and other than unstressed final /e/); stress falls on the penult when the word ends in /ɔ/ (pp. 57, 58, 60) or in unstressed final /e/, which the source gives for monomorphemic nouns as well as verbs (61f-h álbe 'trough', dýbe 'doubt', htábe placename, p. 57; verbal (me) dórme 'I sleep', p. 60). Cresci analyses the unstressed final vowel as extrametrical, its quality tied to extrametricality (pp. 64-65). The /e/ condition is partial: the p. 58 and p. 60 rule statements name only /ɔ/ ('Stress falls on the last syllable of the word if it ends in a segment other than /ɔ/, otherwise on the penult'), and final stressed /e/ occurs (mɛhdé 'noon', ex. 20, p. 38; monosyllables é, dé, p. 64). Small lexical residue: inherited Latin proparoxytones with antepenult stress (mɔnegɔ 'nun', betɔnegɔ 'betony') or penult stress before a final consonant (fórbɛh, pɛten, légor, frángwɛn); the never-stressed suffix /-ol/ and /-ol/-final words (pitɔkol, nígol); the string /-ɛk/, which 'may or may not be stressed' (p. 60); unstressed epenthetic /ɛ/ (mágɛr, ázɛn, kalýz[ɛ]n). Monosyllabic content words, including CV/V ones, are stressed (pp. 56, 63-64).
4114.srule: No word-internal secondary stress: every simplex and suffixed word in §3.3 carries one (primary) stress and §3.6 parses the word as a single right-dominant unbounded foot. 4121.dflt: (Arandic-wide statement) onsetless initial syllable -> stress on the second syllable; nothing stated about disyllables or about Lower Arrernte.
4121.prule: No reachable source states a stress rule for Lower Arrernte itself: Breen 2001's dedicated section 4.11 (rounding moved to consonant onsets, velar glide after /i/) does not discuss stress, and the language is not named in Koch 2014. What the sources state is an Arandic-wide generalisation: main stress on the first syllable that begins with a consonant, i.e. the first vowel preceded by a consonant, which in the mostly vowel-initial Arandic words is normally the second orthographic syllable (equivalently the second syllable over VC(C) syllables, Breen). Breen hedges it as 'the most widespread stress rule in Arandic', Koch 2014 as 'usually', and Yallop 1977:43 (Google Books) says 'Stress patterns are not uniform throughout the Arandic area'. Lower Arrernte is a separate branch of Arandic (Hale 1962 via Koch 2001:72-73; Breen 2001:46 'another separate language'), so the group rule is not attributed to it here.

4122.prule: Primary stress falls on the syllable with a long vowel (written with h) wherever it stands in the word; otherwise on the first syllable ('usually'). No secondary stress is described; 'never (or almost never) two long vowels in a row', and no tie-break is given for a word with two non-adjacent long vowels. Stated by Sharpe 1998 for Yugambeh in a dictionary that covers the neighbouring dialects of a language she says includes Wiyabal (Lismore), Wuhyebal (Coraki) and Nyangbal, i.e. Glottolog's three dialects of lowe1444; Sharpe 1997:372 gives the same analysis (non-initial perceived stress = long vowel) for the whole chain as shared with Crowley and the Geytenbeeks, and 1997:373 invokes 'the stress patterns of the language' to explain vowel shortening in Nyangbal and Wiyabal verb forms. 4123.dq: The prosodic requirement that the minimal word be a bimoraic foot, even when it is a monosyllable, is because a stressed syllable is bimoraic and a prosodic word must have a stressed syllable. (2024: 27) / 'procesos morfológicos como la composición y la adaptación de préstamos recientes revelan su patrón métrico en el nivel de la palabra fonológica' (Hernández Luna 2020: 159)
4123.dloc: 2024 sketch §5 'Prosodic word, syllable structure, and stress', pp. 25-31; cited passage p. 27 (Table 3), summary sentence p. 31. General rule: Hernández Luna 2021 §3 pp. 16-18 (rule statements pp. 16-17; ex. 9 p. 18).
4123.heavy: Not a conditioning factor: the stressed syllable is made bimoraic (vowel lengthening in CV/CVC-lenis, moraic fortis or sonorant coda), and weight follows position. Hernández Luna 2021: 16: isolation [bæːd] 'abeja', [zeːr] 'cera' but compound [bæd.ˈzeːr] 'in which the only bimoraic syllable is the one at the right edge'.
4123.prule: One stressed syllable per prosodic word, on the final syllable of the base (right edge of the prosodic word). The lexicon is mostly monosyllabic; polysyllables (compounds, na- stative forms, recent loans) show an iambic light-heavy pattern with stress on the last syllable; the stressed syllable is bimoraic and unstressed syllables are light. Right-to-left directionality (Hernández Luna 2021 p. 17: 'el acento siempre caerá en la sílaba del borde derecho de la base'), so 3- and 4-syllable compounds also carry a single final stress ([jíð.ŋɡùð.ˈlòː] 'párpado', [jí.síd.ŋɡùð.ˈlòː] 'pestaña'). Enclitics are outside the domain.

4126.heavy: The source states the rule in morae, not in syllable weight: 'it is better to use the mora rather than the syllable as the basic unit'; 'it is appropriate to analyse each nasal in a cluster as one mora' (p. 46); two identical vowels in succession (a vowel Mkude writes double) count two morae ('We must therefore assume another mora between /ló/ and /ka/ in /kolóka/ which can best be represented by doubling the vowel /kolóoka/', p. 39; /líibiki/, /liitúnda/, /lekeléela/, p. 47), and in the four-mora divisions koo/lo/ŋ/ga, koo/hi/n/da (p. 41, stress on lo and hi) each cluster nasal is counted as a mora while the coalesced prefix vowel koo (< ka-o, 'slightly lengthened') is counted as a single mora. Equivalently, heavy syllables = syllables with a double (two-mora) vowel and syllables whose vowel precedes a nasal cluster. Sec. 2.2.1 (p. 43) permits 'Only two types of consonant clusters': '(a) Homorganic nasal + [voiced] stop' and '(b) Consonant + semi-vowel', with nasal + consonant + semi-vowel 'also common' (/mbwali/ 'beer'); the semi-vowel clusters are onsets, so the cluster nasal is the only consonant that contributes a mora; syllabic /m/ from the mu- prefix (classes 1, 3, 18) is a mora on its own (p. 44). Final syllables are open and short in all examples.

4126.prule: Primary stress falls on the third mora from the end of the word. Morae: each short vowel = 1, a long vowel = 2, each nasal in a nasal cluster (NC) = 1, syllabic /m/ (mu- prefix allomorph) = 1. In syllable terms: penultimate stress when the penult is heavy (long vowel: /kolóoka/, /liitúnda/, /lekeléela/; or vowel before a nasal cluster: /iŋómbe/, /iŋánda/, /túnda/, /génda/), antepenultimate when the last three morae are three light syllables (/kólola/, /íŋowo/, /íŋamo/, /lékela/, /lekéleza/), initial in two-mora words (/léka/, /bíki/). Final syllables are open and short in all examples, so the rule never places stress on the final syllable. Stress relocates under prefixation and suffixation only to keep the third-mora count (/bíki/ vs /líibiki/; /léka/, /lékela/, /lekéleza/, /lekeléela/). In one example the third mora is a cluster nasal and Mkude marks stress on it: /geńdela/ 'gend-ela' (p. 47), though p. 44 says a nonsyllabic nasal 'is not capable of bearing stress' (internal tension in the source).
